paras: The reported lynching of Joe Taylor was a mob killing said to have taken place in Texas, apparently at Texarkana, in early November 1888, known only from a dispatch received by Taylor's relatives in West Virginia. One version held that Taylor, accused of shooting a man, was about to be lynched, while a Parkersburg wire said a mob had taken him from prison and hanged him. Papers outside Texas carried the story as news of a native West Virginian, and no report from Texas confirming it appears in the coverage.

Taylor was formerly of Cairo, in Ritchie County, West Virginia. About a year before the reports, he had married Sallie Knight, daughter of Ed. Knight, at Parkersburg and deserted her a few days later. According to the Ritchie Review, he left with a woman from Cairo, and nothing was heard of him afterward.

The Ritchie Review reported that in the preceding week a dispatch reached Taylor's brother Cam saying that Joe had shot a man in "Texarcanna, Tex." and "was about to be lynched." Its editor did not know the outcome but wrote that "we suppose" Taylor had since been hanged. A Parkersburg dispatch gave a fuller account: a relative had been told that Joe had killed a man in Texas and that "a mob had taken him out of prison and hung him." Neither version gave a date, the name of the man shot, the county, or Taylor's race.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no account from Texarkana was found.

The story moved through two channels, both starting with Taylor's family. The Ritchie Review's item, reprinted in the Wheeling Register on November 12 and the Point Pleasant Weekly Register on November 14, dwelt on Taylor's desertion of his young bride and closed by guessing that his "carcass" had been "hung up as food for the buzzards." The Wheeling Register ran it under the heading "A West Virginian in Trouble," but its column deck announced "A West Virginian Lynched."

The Parkersburg wire, stating the lynching as fact on the relatives' word, appeared as "West Virginian Lynched in Texas" in the Clarksville Evening Chronicle on November 13 and the Macon Beacon on November 17. The two printings carried different datelines, November 13 and November 11. Neither channel added comment on the shooting or on the mob.

The accounts disagree on the central point: the Ritchie Review said Taylor had shot a man and was about to be lynched, while the Parkersburg wire said he had killed a man and was taken from prison and hanged. Both rest on word received by Taylor's relatives rather than on a Texas report, so neither is clearly the better evidence.

reader.title: Reported lynching of Joe Taylor
bases: A Parkersburg wire reported that a mob took Taylor out of prison in Texas and hanged him (A2), while the Ritchie Review item said only that he was about to be lynched (A1).

The wire says a mob took Taylor from prison and hanged him for killing a man (A2), but the earlier Ritchie Review version says he was only about to be lynched and guesses at the outcome (A1); both rest on a dispatch to Taylor's relatives, and no Texas report confirms a killing.
Both versions trace to a dispatch received by Taylor's family in West Virginia (A1, A2); they disagree on whether the lynching happened, and no report from Texarkana or anywhere in Texas was found.

accounts.label: Ritchie Review (local W. Va. weekly)
accounts.gist: A dispatch to Taylor's brother Cam said Joe had shot a man in Texarkana, Tex., and was about to be lynched; the editor supposed he had since been hanged.

accounts.label: Parkersburg wire
accounts.gist: A dispatch to one of Taylor's relatives said he had killed a man in Texas and that a mob had taken him out of prison and hanged him.

framing.detail: The Ritchie Review item dwelt on Taylor's desertion of his bride and jeered that his 'carcass' was likely 'food for the buzzards'; the Wheeling Register's deck turned 'about to be lynched' into 'A West Virginian Lynched'.
The Parkersburg wire, headed 'West Virginian Lynched in Texas', stated the lynching as reported in a family dispatch without comment.
